lines.text: They called it the Winter War. As far as I could tell, it began with a queue.
By the end of my first week as Lord of the North, petitioners stood in the snow from my door to the gate. Most of them wanted something from me personally.
My lord, my goat won't give milk. The priest says it's the war. My wife says it's the goat. You decide.
I ruled in favour of the goat. It seemed the safest side to be on.
There were marriage offers, too. Eleven in one week. Ysolde read them all and sorted them into three piles. Desperate, ambitious, and very desperate.
This one's from the eastern hills. His daughter is forty. He writes that she's very mature for her age.
And then there was Ash.
In the village, a club had formed. Children in black cloaks, one ear folded down, who followed Ash everywhere at a respectful distance and growled at strangers.
Carved Ash, my lord. Five coppers each. The torn ear is extra. I've sold four hundred this week.
Pell, you can't sell my dog.
I'm not selling your dog, my lord. I'm selling his likeness. Loyal to profit, remember?
Ash's mate refused to look at him for a whole day, to punish him for leaving. On the third day, the pups were allowed to climb on him again.
Something touched him, Lucan. Under the cathedral. That white isn't a scar. And for weeks, something hid his thread from everyone. Even from you.
I remembered a thin hand reaching through iron bars in the dark, to rest on his head, right where the white began.
Keep him warm, she had said.
Then the war council began. Halvard wanted to march south and burn Aldcrown. Ysolde wanted to know who would carry the bread.
Give me a thousand men and a month, and I'll knock on Vance's door with my sword.
You'll knock with an empty stomach, my lord. A thousand men eat four tons of bread a week. I counted.
I'm not giving myself up. And I won't burn a city full of people who never did anything to me. There has to be a third way.
We get my father out. Quietly. Before midwinter.
War doesn't wait for clever plans, my lord. The King will send another army north either way. You'll need both. A plan, and an army.
He was right. I had a clever plan. What I didn't have was an army. I had farmers, and hunters, and fishermen, and a lot of children dressed as my dog.
That night, I opened the Charter of Aldric again. Two pages after the Fourth Article was a sentence I'd been saving.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter one hundred and twenty-two, coming soon.
